deckName: KS3 DT · J3 Lesson 3 — Playlist Engine (Teacher Deck)

slides.kicker: OUR LADY'S GRAMMAR SCHOOL · DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY
slides.heading: Lesson 3 · Playlist Engine
slides.sub: One name. A whole set of things. — J3 · Lesson 3 of 17
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: coming in, logging in, opening the class link from Google Classroom. The lesson opens on the Do-Now — questions from the last two lessons that mark themselves as each pupil answers them. Nothing in it is graded and nothing about it is shown to the class.

SAY: "Log in, open the class link, and work through the warm-up on your own screen. When it hands you over to today's first card, stop and look up."

WHY: it is revision, and it gives you a settled room to take the register in.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room is on today's first card, stop everybody, eyes front, and go on.

slides.heading: In this lesson you will…
bullets: Keep a whole set of things under one name.
Take one out, count them, add one on the end, and put them in order.
Say what a line of Python is going to print BEFORE it runs.
Write the program that runs a playlist, from nothing.
slides.notes:
SAY these as written. The third one is the odd one out and it is deliberate: predicting is a skill in its own right, and the Match is fifteen minutes of practising it.

WHY IT MATTERS: up to now one name has held one thing. Today one name holds twenty. Almost everything they will ever write afterwards depends on that.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: The one new idea today
bullets: A name can hold a whole set of things at once, in order.
The places are numbered, and the numbering starts at 0.
You can take one out, count them, add one on, and sort them.
Everything else about writing Python is what you already do.
slides.notes:
SAY it as written. The 0 is worth saying twice — it is the single thing this hour goes wrong on, and the film spends a whole part on it.

DO NOT call it a list yet if you can help it. The film builds the picture first — a rack of numbered boxes — and the word lands better after the picture.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: How the hour is laid out
bullets: A short film, then straight into the Match against a partner.
A second short film, then three builds.
Then twelve minutes writing the playlist engine — no pieces, you type it.
Two short screens at the end.
slides.notes:
SAY it as written. The Match coming early is unusual and worth flagging, because a room that expects to build first will be thrown by it.

WHY THE MATCH IS EARLY: it is fifteen minutes of reading Python closely, against somebody. Everything they build afterwards is easier for having done it.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: Two things before we start
bullets: No music plays today. Nothing here makes a sound.
The playlist is a set of song names in a program — that is all.
In the Match you are guessing what Python will print, not racing.
Getting one wrong costs you nothing. There is no penalty anywhere in it.
slides.notes:
SAY the first two now, before anybody asks. Every class asks whether real music plays, and the answer landing early saves you three interruptions later.

SAY: "The Match is not a race. You are working out what a line of Python is going to print, and you get as long as you need."

WHEN TO MOVE: on to the film slide, then let them go.

slides.heading: The first film — on your own screen
bullets: It plays on your own computer, not on the board.
No sound, so every word you need is written on the screen.
Four parts, and the buttons underneath jump to any part.
Just under four minutes.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to start the first film on their own machines.

SAY: "The film is on your screen, not mine. It has no sound at all. It is just under four minutes long, in four parts, and the buttons underneath take you back to any of them."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: a player with four buttons under it, named "One box, then a rack of them", "Counting starts at 0", "How many things are in the list?" and "Adding one on the end". A pupil can jump to any part while she is on this screen.

DO NOT play it on the board — it is written to be read at each pupil's own pace.

WHILE IT RUNS: walk the room and check everybody is on it. You will want the room together for the next slide.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room is past it. Pull the stragglers up — the Match needs everybody at once.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The Match
bullets: You are about to be given a partner. The website chooses.
You are not told who they are, and they are not told who you are.
You each get a call sign — Director 3, Editor 5 — and that is what you are.
Six rounds. You both say what a line of Python will print.
You both commit first, THEN you see each other's. Nobody copies.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: first film finished, eyes front, everybody together. THIS SLIDE IS THE ONE TO SLOW DOWN ON, especially the first time you run a paired activity.

SAY: "In a moment the website pairs you with somebody else in this room. You do not choose and I do not choose — it pairs whoever is ready at the same time."

THEN SAY: "You are not told who your partner is and they are not told who you are. You get a call sign instead — Director 3, Editor 5, and so on. The screen tells you yours."

THEN SAY, and this is the part that makes it work: "You will both see the same line of Python. You each say what you think it prints. Neither of you sees the other's answer until you have BOTH said yours. So there is no point waiting to see what they put."

THEN SAY: "Then the line actually runs, and you both find out."

ONE ROUND HAS NO OPTIONS: on round 2 neither pupil is given answers to choose from — they type what they think it prints. Say so; a pupil who expects buttons and gets a typing box wastes half a minute working it out.

THE LAST TWO ROUNDS ARE MEANT TO BE GOT WRONG. Rounds 5 and 6 are on a loop and on sort, and nothing has taught either. Each one puts a GUESS ROUND banner up before it starts, saying nobody has taught this yet and there are no points either way. Expect a room full of wrong answers there and say beforehand that this is the design, not a test — round 6 in particular catches nearly everybody, and the second film explains it straight afterwards.

IF THE CLASS IS AN ODD NUMBER: the website holds the last three and puts them in one group of three. You do not have to do anything.

IF SOMEBODY IS STILL WAITING: they are not stuck, and they do not need you. A cartoon theatre critic called Margo keeps them company, and after a short wait the screen itself offers "Play the computer" — that pupil then plays all six rounds on their own screen and keeps the badge. Nothing here needs a teacher to release it, which is what makes it safe on a cover day.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: While you wait
bullets: You might have to wait for somebody to play against. Nothing is wrong: stay on this screen.
While you wait, a cartoon theatre critic called Margo keeps you company.
The moment somebody is ready, the screen changes by itself.
If you have waited a long time, the screen offers you a button marked Play the computer. Press it and you play all six rounds on your own.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: pupils finish the film at different times, so they reach the Match at different times — the first ones through will wait.

SAY it with the picture up: "If you get this screen, you are in the queue and nothing is wrong. The website matches whoever is ready at the same time. Margo is there to keep you company."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the waiting card, with Margo on it. She mostly talks to herself and is not a real chatbot, though she has one line for anything a pupil types at her — and she vanishes the moment an opponent arrives.

IF SOMEBODY IS STILL WAITING: they do not need you. After a longer wait the screen itself offers "Play the computer", which runs all six rounds on that pupil's own screen, badge included. Nothing on this screen needs a teacher to release it.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: You have an opponent
bullets: This card appears the moment the website has found you somebody to play against.
The screen tells you your opponent's call sign. It also tells you what you are called on their screen.
Real names stay secret — theirs and yours — until the Match ends.
Press Start the Match. You both see the same code at the same moment.
slides.notes:
SAY it with the picture up: "This is the card you get when you have an opponent. It tells you their call sign and yours. That is the only name either of you sees until the Match is over. Press Start the Match."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the MATCHED card, with two call signs on it — hers, and her opponent's. The names on the picture are examples: every pair gets its own.

THE ONE TO STRESS: real names stay out of everything until the Match ends, when the screen tells each pupil who she was playing. You can see who is matched with whom on the Live tab, by call sign with real names in brackets.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: What the Match looks like
bullets: The lines of Python are in the middle of the card. Read them before you choose.
You choose or type what it prints, then press Lock in my prediction.
Once you lock in, the answers switch off and the screen waits for your opponent.
When you have both locked in, the code runs for real, and both predictions sit beside what it really printed.
Getting one wrong costs you nothing. Read the line that explains it, then press Next round.
slides.notes:
SAY the bullets aloud, naming each part of the screen as you reach it. There is deliberately no picture of a round on this slide: any round photographed shows that round's code and its answer, and the Match is played after this slide.

THE ONE TO STRESS: the reveal is the line really running. It is not a stored answer and it is not marking — the class is watching Python do it.

AND: locking in is final for that round, and nothing is shown until both have done it — so there is nothing to gain by waiting to see what the other one puts.

IF A PAIR DISAGREES AND BOTH ARE WRONG: that is the best thing that can happen and it is worth saying so. Nothing is deducted.

WHAT YOU CAN SEE: on the Live tab, the Pairing panel shows who is paired with whom, by call sign with real names in brackets, and Channel opens what a pair has sent each other.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in. This runs about eleven minutes.

slides.heading: The second film
bullets: Again on your own screen, again no sound.
It picks up exactly where the Match left off.
Three parts. Just under four minutes.
It includes the one that caught nearly everybody.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: Match finished. Some pairs will be talking about the round that caught them — let that run for fifteen seconds, it is the point of the activity.

SAY: "This is the second film, and it works like the first: it is on your screen, it has no sound, and it is just under four minutes long. It carries straight on from the Match, and it explains the round that caught most of the room."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: a player with three buttons under it, named "Taking one out", "Taking just the first three" and "Putting the titles in order, and the trap that catches people".

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room is past it.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The three builds
bullets: Three builds, and they get harder.
The first is written for you: read it and run it.
The second is in pieces and you put it in order.
The third is the one that carries the badge.
All three RUN. If one stops, read the plain line under the red.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: second film finished, eyes front. One minute here saves you ten walking the room.

SAY: "Three builds. The first is already written — read it and run it. The second is in pieces. The third is yours to work out and it is the one that carries the badge."

ABOUT THE THIRD BUILD: six lines are on the card and four of them make the working program — the job is to use all four. Two are there to be read and left alone: one uses a word lists do not have, and one asks for position 3 in a list of three. The title added by the append line is the pupil's own to invent, so no two programs read the same. And a pupil who prints the right number using only two lines is refused by the card itself, with a message saying which lines the job asks for — so "but it printed 3" is answered on screen before it reaches you.

DO NOT walk anybody through the third from the front.

SAY ABOUT ERRORS: "When a program stops, Python puts up a red message and there is a plain English line underneath it. Read that line first."

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: What a build screen looks like
bullets: The program is on the left. The console is on the right.
RUN is at the bottom. Nothing happens until it is pressed.
The console shows exactly what your program printed. The first build prints Now Playing and three titles.
If Python stops, the console goes red. Read the plain line under the red first.
slides.notes:
SAY it with the picture up, pointing at each part.

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the first build after its run — the six lines on the left, and on the right the console printing Now Playing - Top 3 and three titles, with IT WORKS underneath. That console is the shape of every playlist engine in the hour: make the list, add one, take one out, print the first three.

THE ONE TO STRESS: the console shows what the program REALLY did. When it is not what the target says, read the console and the lines above it side by side, and find the first line that is different.

SAY ABOUT ERRORS: "When a program stops, Python puts up a red message and there is a plain English line underneath it. Read that line first."

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: The lines are in the wrong order
bullets: In Build 3 you get six lines. They sit on the left in a mixed-up order. Two of them do not belong in the program. The order they sit in is not a clue. You work out the right order yourself.
Four of the six make the working program. Two are there to be read and left alone.
Click a line to move it into Your program, or drag it. Some lines have gaps you type into.
To take a line back, press the button beside it that says Put this line back.
RUN switches on as soon as there is at least one line in Your program.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to open the third build, the one that carries a badge.

SAY it with the picture up, pointing at each part: "The six lines are on the left, and your program is on the right. Four of them make the working program and two are wrong on purpose. The order on the left is not a hint. You work out the correct order yourself."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the third build before a line has been moved — six shuffled lines with their gaps, the empty program, and the RUN button still switched off.

THE ONE TO STRESS: the platform shuffles the lines on THIS build afresh every time the card opens, for every pupil — the screen does not announce this, but it is true — so two neighbours see different orders, and the position of a line on the next desk tells her nothing. That is worth saying out loud, kindly, once. The second build is different: its four lines sit in the same order for everybody, and each pupil gets one go at it.

DO NOT walk the class through Build 3 from the front of the room. They do it themselves.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The engine
bullets: Twelve minutes. You type this one — there are no pieces to drag.
Five jobs: add a song, take one out, pick one at random, put them in A to Z order, and print Now Playing with the first three.
The random one uses Python nobody has shown you. The card teaches it before you need it.
Your five jobs sit along the top of the card, and they tick only after you press RUN.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: the three builds finished, eyes front. This is the biggest block of the hour and the hardest, and the room needs to know what finished looks like.

SAY: "You have twelve minutes, and you type this one from scratch — there are no lines to drag. It has five jobs to do, and they are listed across the top of the card so you can see which ones you have done."

THEN SAY: "Those five are not read off your program. They watch your program while it runs. So if you have written the right thing and it still says NOT YET — have you pressed RUN since you changed it?"

THAT ONE SENTENCE answers most of what you will be asked in the next twelve minutes.

THE ONE PIECE OF NEW PYTHON: the third job picks a song at random, and nothing before this hour has taught that. The card teaches it at the top, in two lines — import random on the very first line of the program, and random.choice(playlist) to pick one title out. You do not need to teach it from the front; you do need to know it is there, because it is the job pupils ask about.

ABOUT THE TWO PARTS: the card shows one thing at a time. The first face says what she is making before anything can be typed; Start writing gives her the page where she types, and the console is not on that page until she presses RUN. The next two slides are those two faces.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide, then walk the room.

slides.heading: First you plan
bullets: The card starts by showing you the goal and the five jobs, in the order you do them.
Read the five jobs before you type anything. They are what the card checks.
Press the button marked Start writing. The card turns into the page where you type.
slides.notes:
SAY, with the picture up: "The card starts by telling you what your engine has to do — five jobs, in order. When you press Start writing, the card turns into the page where you type, and those same five jobs move up to the top so you can see them the whole time."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the PLAN face — the goal, the five jobs, and the Start writing button. Nothing can be typed on this face, and that is deliberate: she reads what the engine has to do before she can start.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: Then you type
bullets: You type your program into the black space. It numbers your lines for you.
Tab moves you four spaces in — that is how lines go inside a loop.
The five jobs are along the top. Each job ticks when your program really does that job.
If you are stuck, press Show me the shape or Write the shape for me. You lose no points for using either.
slides.notes:
SAY it with the picture up.

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the page where she types, before a character has been typed — the five jobs along the top, the empty box with its line numbers, and the help row under it.

ABOUT THE HELP: everything on that card is free — no points are taken for opening any of it, and nobody is shown who used it. Say that plainly. A pupil who thinks help costs her something will sit and do nothing instead, which costs her more.

IF THE RANDOM JOB WILL NOT TICK, it is one of two things and the card's own nudge says both: the first line of the program has to read import random, and the line that prints Tonight has to use random.choice. Ask which of the two is missing rather than reading the program yourself.

ABOUT INDENTING: Tab puts four spaces in. Pupils who have only ever dragged blocks have never had to indent anything, and this is the first hour they meet it.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in.

slides.heading: The last three screens
bullets: First a screen of three extra jobs. They are optional and none of them is marked.
Then one question about append. That one IS marked.
Then you put three short lines of Python in the right order. You get one go, and you are shown the working order afterwards.
You are told how you did at the very end, not as you go.
Then How did it go? Nobody leaves without finishing it.
slides.notes:
SAY: "One marked question, then a short ordering puzzle. You are told whether you were right, and why, at the very end of the lesson — after the How did it go? screen."

ABOUT THE COMMENT BOX on the How did it go? screen: it goes to you and to nobody else.

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the extra-jobs screen — three jobs, none of them ticked, and the button at the bottom that carries her straight on.

EXTRA JOBS: every pupil lands on the extra-jobs screen after the engine — it is not a reward for finishing early. There are three of them, they carry no points at all, nothing there is marked or saved, and a button on it carries a pupil straight on. Say so, or a pupil who thinks she is missing marks will rush what matters.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the closer.

slides.heading: Before you leave
bullets: Finish How did it go? Nobody leaves without it.
Sign out every time. Anything the next person does looks like you.
Your playlist engine is saved. It will still be there next lesson.
slides.notes:
SAY the sign-out line every lesson without exception. On shared C2k machines it is the single habit that matters most.

SAY: "Your engine is saved. You do not need to write it down or email it to yourself."

LAST THING: if the Match went well, say so. It is the first time these pupils have worked against a partner they could not see, and a sentence about how they handled it makes the next one easier to run.
